steps.observation: Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
Elias Maples had tended Tangle Point Lighthouse for nearly twenty years. Each dawn he climbed the narrow spiral stairs, wind tugging at his oilskin coat, to polish the great Fresnel lens until it gleamed like a moonlit promise. Below him, breakers thundered against jagged rocks; the gulls wheeled and screamed, as though warning mariners of hidden shoals.

When storms rolled in—dark clouds hemming the horizon, sheets of rain rattling the windows—Elias would stoke the lantern’s lamp, its beam cutting a steady path through the tempest. He remembered the first ship he’d rescued here: nearly forty years old now, the veteran seaman still lived in the fishing village and wrote Elias every Christmas. “Your light saved us,” the old captain had scribbled on yellowed paper. Those words warmed Elias more than any hearth.

Loneliness was his constant companion. Evenings, he sat at a rough-hewn table, a single candle flickering beside a steaming mug of tea. He wrote letters he never mailed, jotting down dreams of travel and laughter—things he’d never tasted but never ceased to imagine. Sometimes he spoke aloud, recounting stories for an audience of wall-mounted oilskins and sea charts. The walls themselves seemed to listen.

One night, as a gale tore at the windows, Elias detected a faint horn in the howl of wind. He plunged outside, flashlight in one hand, and saw the silhouette of a small fishing boat caught in the surf. Heart pounding, he sounded the foghorn and flung distress flares skyward. Minutes later, he guided the battered crew to shore with the unerring beam of his lamp. They reached the rocks trembling but alive.

Back in the lantern room, Elias extinguished the flares, watched the horizon calm, and allowed himself a small, satisfied smile. Though the sea was vast and unyielding, the lighthouse endured—and so did he, its faithful guardian, keeping hope alive for every soul lost in the dark.
